note: Etiquette/behavior sense: borrowed refined ways, politeness

replacement: In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to draw two clearly separate lines of action for the two sexes and to have them keep pace with each other, but on paths that are always different. American women never manage the family’s outside affairs, or run a business, or take part in political life. Nor, on the other hand, are they ever forced to do the rough labor of the fields or any of those heavy tasks that demand physical strength. No family is so poor as to be an exception to this rule. If an American woman cannot escape the quiet circle of domestic occupations, neither is she ever forced to go beyond it. So it is that the women of America, who often show a masculine strength of understanding and a manly energy, generally keep great delicacy of personal appearance and always keep the habits of women, although they sometimes prove that they have the hearts and minds of men.

note: mœurs sense in list of shared way of life
replacement: One might suppose that the final consequence and necessary effect of democratic institutions is to throw all members of the community together in private as well as public life, and to force them all to live in common. But that would be to give the equality that arises from democracy a very crude and oppressive form. No state of society and no laws can make men so alike that education, fortune, and tastes will not put some differences between them. And although different men may sometimes find it in their interest to combine for the same purposes, they will never make it their pleasure. They will therefore always tend to evade the provisions of the law, whatever those may be. Departing in some one respect from the circle within which they were meant to be confined, they will set up, close beside the great political community, small private circles united by the similarity of their conditions, habits, and customs.

note: mœurs sense: way of life of the small circles
replacement: In aristocracies men are separated from one another by lofty, fixed barriers; in democracies they are divided by a multitude of small, almost invisible threads, which are constantly broken or moved from place to place. Thus, whatever the progress of equality, a great number of small private communities will always form within the general bounds of political society in democratic nations. But none of them will resemble in its customs the highest class in aristocracies.
